land.text: the Ming lands Li Zicheng took: Xiangyang ('By 1643, Li had captured Xiangyang'), Xi'an and Shaanxi (late 1643), Taiyuan (March 1644) and Beijing (April 1644)

predecessors.note: A rebel state carved from the Ming; the dossier starts when the pages first give him land.

land.text: Beijing (6 June 1644), then Xi'an and Shaanxi when Li 'abandon[ed] his headquarters in Xi'an in February 1645'

successors.note: The qing-dynasty dossier records the Shun as the counterpart of its 1644 gains in North China.

land.text: Hubei, where Li 'is generally believed to have died ... in 1645'; the Shun page: 'Surrender to the Southern Ming: 1646'

successors.note: The remnant armies, not land: the Shun page dates the end of the dynasty to 1649 (Li Guo died at Nanning, Guangxi).

capitals.name: Xi'an (Xijing)
capitals.note: Infobox 'Capital: Xi'an (1644)'; Li entered Xi'an in late 1643 and founded the Shun there on 8 February 1644.

capitals.name: Beijing
capitals.note: Infobox 'Beijing (1644 - 5 June 1644)'; captured in April, Li proclaimed himself emperor there on 3 June.

capitals.name: Xi'an
capitals.note: 'When Wu Sangui and Prince Dorgon took control of Beijing, Li Zicheng fled to Xi'an'; abandoned in February 1645.

rulers.name: Li Zicheng (Yongchang Emperor from 1644)
rulers.title: Dashing King, then emperor of the Shun
rulers.note: Era name Yongchang 1644-1645; founding 8 February 1644, enthronement 3 June 1644 (infobox); died in Hubei in 1645, circumstances unclear.

correction.text: Not Shun land: Li Zicheng led a rebel band, not a territory, in 1632-1635; the area belongs to the Ming

keyframe_review.note: 38,974 km2 of northern Shaanxi (Yulin-Yan'an) for 1632-1635. The Li Zicheng page has him in 1629-30 at Yuzhong and Mizhi, then 'among the forces under the leadership of Gao Yingxiang' about 1633: a rebel band, holding no named land. The patch is Ming land; no Shun territory exists before 1643.

correction.text: Not Shun land: Shanxi and northern Shaanxi were Ming until 1643-44

keyframe_review.note: 259,317 km2 (Shanxi, northern Shaanxi) for 1636-1641 is wrong: the page has Li Zicheng trapped and destroyed in 1638 ('escaped with just 17 followers'), back in Henan in 1639 and sacking the Shaolin Monastery in 1641; Taiyuan fell to him only in March 1644 (Qing conquest page). The land is Ming.

correction.text: Shape unchanged; it holds only from March 1644 (Taiyuan) to the retreat of June 1644

keyframe_review.note: 407,378 km2 (Shaanxi, Shanxi, Henan, northern Hubei) for 1642-1644. It is a fair picture of the Shun in spring 1644 after Taiyuan (March), but not of 1642-43, when the page has the Kaifeng siege (1642), Xiangyang (1643) and Xi'an (late 1643); the years it belongs to are March to June 1644 (new keyframe li-zicheng_1644). The page gives no area to check it against.

correction.text: Xiangyang in Hubei and, late in the year, Xi'an and Shaanxi

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for the first year of land: Xiangyang ('By 1643, Li had captured Xiangyang') and, late in the year, Xi'an and Shaanxi ('Li Zicheng proceeded again to Xi'an'). Henan is not claimed: the page has the sieges of Luoyang and Kaifeng (1641-42) but no capture of the province.

correction.text: Shaanxi, Shanxi, Henan and northern Hubei of Cliopatria's 1642 shape plus Beijing, from the fall of Taiyuan (March 1644) to the retreat of June 1644

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for the Shun at its height: Cliopatria's 1642 shape (Shaanxi, Shanxi, Henan, northern Hubei) plus Beijing. 'In March, his armies had captured the important city of Taiyuan in Shanxi'; Beijing in April; Li fled from Beijing in June and the Shanhai Pass battle was lost on 27 May. The page gives no area; the Shun page says only that it 'controlled much of North China for a short period'.

New keyframe for the end: after Beijing was lost (June 1644) Li 'fled to Xi'an', and was 'forc[ed] ... to abandon his headquarters in Xi'an in February 1645'. The page does not say what else the Shun held in the interval; Shanxi and Henan were lost to the Qing in 1644-45 (page silent), so only Shaanxi is kept.

ledger.note: 1643: Li Zicheng, in rebellion since 1629, holds Xiangyang. 'By 1643, Li had captured Xiangyang'; the page's lead gives 1643 and the Cliopatria shape begins in 1642. The page does not say a state was proclaimed at Xiangyang, so the founding year is the year of the first land.
1643: Li Zicheng takes Xi'an and Shaanxi. 'After assigned his subordinate to command Tongguan, Li Zicheng proceeded again to Xi'an' in late 1643; the page gives no month for the entry.

1644: Li Zicheng founds the Great Shun at Xi'an. 'On the Chinese New Year, which fell on 8 February, Li declared the founding of the "Great Shun" dynasty in Xi'an'; infobox 'Established in Xi'an: 8 February 1644', era name Yongchang. Same state, same colour.
1644: Li Zicheng's armies take Taiyuan and Shanxi. 'In March, his armies had captured the important city of Taiyuan in Shanxi.' The page names the city, the province is the reading.

1644: Beijing falls to Li Zicheng. 'The gates of Beijing were opened from the inside, allowing Li's forces to capture the city' (24 April on the Qing conquest page, 25 April on the Ming page); the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself the next day.
1644: the Shun capital moves from Xi'an to Beijing. Infobox 'Capital: Xi'an (1644) Beijing (1644 - 5 June 1644)'; Li proclaimed himself emperor there on 3 June.
1644: the Shun and Wu Sangui fight at Shanhai Pass. 'Wu's battle-hardened troops defeated them easily on 5 May and 10 May.' The zone is the pass and the corridor to Beijing.

1644: Li is beaten at Shanhai Pass. 'Li's army was eventually defeated on 27 May 1644'; 'After Wu formally surrendered to the Qing in the morning of 27 May, his elite troops charged the rebel army repeatedly.'

1644: the Shun lose Beijing. Li proclaimed himself emperor on 3 June (infobox) and fled; 'On 6 June, the mainly Han Chinese forces of Dorgon and Wu entered the capital.' The Shun page puts the fall of Beijing on 5 June.

region.text: Shanxi, Henan and northern Hubei: page silent

ledger.note: 1645: North China is the Qing's, bridging (by 1645). After Beijing 'Li Zicheng fled to Xi'an'; Shanxi and Henan are no longer Shun land by 1645 in the Cliopatria Qing shape, but no page opened dates them.
1645: Li abandons Xi'an. The Qing advance forced 'Li Zicheng to abandon his headquarters in Xi'an in February 1645'; 'he is generally believed to have died in Hubei in 1645'.

region.text: the Shun at its largest, abandoned by February 1645

ledger.note: 1645: the Shun end as a territory. 'The Shun dynasty weakened dramatically after the death of Li Zicheng in 1645'; the remnant armies joined the Southern Ming (Shun page 'Surrender to the Southern Ming: 1646') and the dynasty is dated to 1649, when Li Guo died at Nanning.

wars.name: Battle of Shanhai Pass
wars.outcome: Wu Sangui opened the pass to the Manchus; Li's army was defeated on 27 May 1644 and Beijing was lost on 5-6 June.
wars.note: Battles on 5 and 10 May and the decisive one on 27 May.

wars.name: Late Ming peasant rebellions
wars.outcome: Li Zicheng rose at Mizhi in 1629, was destroyed in 1638, rebuilt his army in Henan from 1639, took Xiangyang (1643), Xi'an (late 1643) and Beijing (April 1644).

wars.name: Qing pursuit of the Shun
wars.outcome: Li was forced out of Xi'an in February 1645 and is thought to have died in Hubei that year.

certainty.note: A mobile rebel regime: the land held changes with the armies' positions; no page gives a boundary.

notes:
Written by ea-07 on 2026-10-25 from the four pages in sources (page budget 1-2; the Qing conquest and Ming pages are shared with the other dossiers of the group). This is the Shun of Li Zicheng, type rebel; Cliopatria's row 'Li Zicheng' is the only Cliopatria record of it.

Cliopatria problems. The 1632-1635 and 1636-1641 shapes (northern Shaanxi, then Shanxi and Shaanxi) are wrong: the Li Zicheng page has a roving rebel band (Mizhi 1629, under Gao Yingxiang about 1633, destroyed 1638, Henan 1639), and Shanxi was Ming until March 1644; the same cells are missing from Cliopatria's Ming shapes of 1632-1641 (see ming-dynasty). The 1642-1644 shape is a fair picture of the Shun of spring 1644 only. New keyframes cover 1643, 1644 and 1645.

Not settled: when and where Li proclaimed the Xinshun kingdom (the pages say only 'By 1643, Li had captured Xiangyang', so the founding year is the first-land year, confidence 2); whether Henan was ever held (Luoyang and Kaifeng were sacked or besieged 1641-42, no capture dated); Datong and Xuanfu in March 1644 (page silent); the dating of the Shun's loss of Shanxi and Henan (June 1644 to February 1645, page silent, confidence 1); the Shun's end (1645 for the territory; the Shun page says 1649, Li Guo's death at Nanning, and 1646 for the surrender of the remnants to the Southern Ming); no page gives an area. Pages disagree on the day Beijing fell (24 April on the Qing conquest page, 25 April on the Ming page; the Shun page lists 'Fall of Beijing: 5 June 1644', which is the Shun losing it). Gazetteer names all resolve (Xian, Xiangyang, Qinhuangdao for Shanhai Pass). The Qing dossier (ea-08) uses the string 'Shun regime of Li Zicheng' as counterpart; it should read li-zicheng.
